aoi.description: Select the area you want to analyse. All subsequent steps will be clipped to this boundary.

variables.description: Add input variables for the risk model.
variables.info_md:
Source variables are the input layers the risk model is built from. Add them from two sources:

- **predefined** — ready-made layers fetched from [Google Earth Engine](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets) and clipped to your AOI. Each comes from a published global dataset: elevation and slope (NASA SRTM), forest cover (Hansen Global Forest Change or JRC Tropical Moist Forest), protected areas (WDPA), rivers and roads (OpenStreetMap), towns (JRC GHSL) and subjurisdictions (FAO GAUL). Select one in the Add Variable dialog to see exactly how it is generated and where the data comes from.
- **custom** — your own data: a local GeoTIFF raster, a local vector file (GeoJSON/GPKG/SHP — rasterized during processing), or any GEE image asset you have access to.

Temporal variables (e.g. forest cover) carry a year, so the same layer can be added for several years. All layers are brought onto one common grid in Step 3 — Process.

variables.confirm_remove_base_warning: It is the base raster's source, so the base raster will also be cleared.
variables.error_no_project: No active project — complete the AOI step first.
variables.error_base_raster_reset: Base raster was reset because its source layer '{name}' changed — re-set it in Step 3 — Process.
variables.error_base_raster_removed: Base raster was reset because its source layer '{name}' was removed — re-set it in Step 3 — Process.

process.description: Download layers, set the base raster + projection, then reproject and rasterize all variables.
process.info_md:
This step brings every source variable onto one common analysis grid:

1. **Download layers** — each GEE-backed variable is exported from Earth Engine and saved as a local GeoTIFF. Local files are used as-is.
2. **Base & projection** — pick one raster as the **base raster**: it defines the grid (CRS, pixel size and extent) every other layer is aligned to. Choose the layer whose spatial detail matters most — typically the forest-cover layer the deforestation target is derived from. Use a projected CRS in metres; **Auto (UTM)** suggests the UTM zone of the layer.
3. **Run processing** — every raster is reprojected and resampled onto the base grid, and vector layers are rasterized onto it. Afterwards all processed layers overlap pixel-by-pixel (same CRS, resolution and extent), which model training and prediction require.

Re-run processing whenever you add or change source variables.
process.base_raster_hint: Defines the analysis grid (CRS, pixel size, extent) all layers are aligned to.
process.epsg_hint: Projected CRS in metres — Auto (UTM) suggests one.
process.resolution_hint: Pixel size in metres for all processed layers.
process.run_processing_subtitle: Aligns every variable onto the base grid: missing GEE layers are downloaded, rasters are reprojected and resampled to the base CRS and resolution, and vector layers are rasterized. The results become the processed variables used by the next steps.
process.error_no_base: Set a base raster above to enable processing.

postprocess.description: Derive new variables from the processed, aligned layers: change detection (loss/gain) and edge/distance transforms.
postprocess.info_md:
Post-processing derives new model inputs from the processed, aligned layers:

- **Change detection (loss / gain)** — compares two presence masks of the same phenomenon at two years and outputs a change mask (1 = event, 0 = stable, 255 = nodata). *loss* marks pixels present at the start but absent at the end (e.g. deforestation between two forest-cover years — the usual model target); *gain* marks the reverse (e.g. regrowth).
- **edge** — for each pixel *inside* a binary mask (value 1), the distance in metres to the mask's edge. Applied to a forest mask it gives distance-to-forest-edge, a key deforestation predictor.
- **dist** — for each pixel *outside* the mask, the distance in metres to the nearest mask pixel. Applied to roads, rivers or towns it gives distance-to-road / river / town.

Both transforms expect a binary (0/1) mask and produce a continuous raster. Results appear in the derived-variables list below and can be used as dataset features (Step 5).
postprocess.change_help_text: Pick two presence masks (1 = present, 0 = absent) of the same phenomenon at two different years — same or different sources. Output: 1 = event, 0 = stable, 255 = nodata.
postprocess.op_hint_loss: 1 where present at start but gone at the end (e.g. deforestation).
postprocess.op_hint_gain: 1 where absent at start but present at the end (e.g. regrowth).
postprocess.processed_variable_hint: Input — a binary (0/1) mask, e.g. forest cover or roads.
postprocess.step_hint_edge: Distance to the mask edge, inside the mask (e.g. distance to forest edge).
postprocess.step_hint_dist: Distance to the nearest mask pixel, outside it (e.g. distance to roads).

dataset.description: Bundle the layers a model learns from: one target (what to predict) and the features (the predictors).
dataset.info_md:
A dataset names the layers a model trains and predicts on:

- **Target** — the variable the model learns to predict: a binary event mask where **1 = event** and 0 = no event. Typically a deforestation *loss* layer generated in Step 4 — Post-process from two forest-cover years.
- **Features** — the explanatory layers the model relates to the target: altitude, slope, distance to forest edge / roads / rivers / towns, protected areas, etc.
- **Year** — when the target or features are temporal (one layer per year), the year selects which annual layer each variable contributes.

Registering validates that every layer exists on disk and shares the common grid from Step 3. Create separate datasets for calibration and validation periods so you can train on one and evaluate on the other.
dataset.target_hint: What the model predicts — a binary mask where 1 = event (e.g. deforestation).
dataset.features_hint: Predictor layers the model uses to explain the target.
dataset.year_hint: Which annual layer temporal variables contribute to this dataset.

sampling.description: Draw a persistent, named sample from a raster variable. Samples are selectable in Train (Step 7) and can be added to the map.
sampling.info_md:
A sample is a saved set of point locations drawn from the pixels of a raster variable; models later extract their training data at these points (Step 6 — Train). Sample types:

- **random** — points drawn uniformly at random among valid pixels.
- **stratified** — the raster's values define classes (strata; e.g. 0/1 of a deforestation mask) and points are drawn per class following the allocation rule: *equal* (total split evenly across classes), *proportional* (split by class pixel count), or *deforisk* (the requested count drawn from **each** class, as in forestatrisk).
- **systematic** — points on a regular grid, defined either by a total count or by the distance between points.

An optional mask restricts sampling to pixels where the mask is non-zero (e.g. forest at period start). The seed makes the draw reproducible.
sampling.raster_variable_hint: Defines valid pixels and, for stratified sampling, the classes (strata).
sampling.mask_variable_hint: Only pixels where this mask is non-zero are sampled (e.g. forest at start).
sampling.strategy_hint_random: Uniform random draw over valid pixels.
sampling.strategy_hint_stratified: Per-class draws based on the raster's values (strata).
sampling.strategy_hint_systematic: Regular grid — by total count or by point spacing.
sampling.allocation_hint_proportional: Total split proportionally to each class's pixel count.
sampling.allocation_hint_deforisk: Draws the requested number from EACH class (forestatrisk-style).
sampling.adapt_label: Adapt allocation to observed deforestation rate
sampling.adapt_hint: Overrides the count: 1000 points per Mha of sampled area, clipped to 10,000–50,000.
sampling.spacing_hint: Grid spacing in metres between neighbouring points.
sampling.n_samples_hint: Total number of points to draw.
sampling.n_samples_hint_deforisk: Points drawn from each class (not a split total).
sampling.seed_hint: Same seed and inputs reproduce the same points.
